newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rights leader sees no "terror" threat to Algeria.
newsitem.headline: Rights leader sees no "terror" threat to Algeria.

text.p: Algeria's government-appointed human rights leader, just hours after 28 people were massacred, said on Sunday that "terrorism" no longer posed a threat to the stability of the country but was a threat to individual safety.

Rezzag Bara, head of the National Observatory of Human Rights, said "criminality and terrorist violence" -- Algeria's official term for attacks by Moslem fundamentalists - were the main threats to human rights, civil peace and protection of life and property.
"Terrorism and acts of sabotage still threaten public security but no longer constitute a danger against the country's stability," Bara was quoted as saying by the official Algerian news agency APS.
"Terrorism and acts of sabotage still threaten public security but no longer constitute a danger against the country's stability," he said.

He did not elaborate. Officials have said that Moslem radicals -- who have staged vicious attacks on civilians over the past few years -- have because of the violence lost support that was reflected in 1991 when the now-banned fundamentalist Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) made a strong showing in polls.

On Sunday, security forces reported that 28 people were massacred in a village in Ain Defla province by a "group of terrorists", and that a bomb had ripped through a cafe in the Algiers suburb of El Harrach. The official toll for the bomb was 20 wounded. Hospital sources said 53 people were wounded.
Bara also criticised the London-based human rights group Amnesty International whose November report spoke of "fear and silence" in Algeria and "a hidden human rights crisis".
Amnesty International had no monopoly on human rights, said Bara.

"Amnesty's latest statements can perfectly be categorised as a cover for the most barbarous terrorist acts, saving neither travellers, passersby, infants, or children. "These statements give to these criminals the stamp of an armed political opposition," Bara said.
Amnesty's report said: "Both security forces and armed opposition groups have shown utter disregard for the most basic human right of the civilian population - the right to life."
The group has also accused Algerian security forces, engaged in a five-year-old conflict with Moslem fundamentalists, of carrying out extra-judicial killings and torture.
About 60,000 people have been killed in violence that erupted shortly after the Algerian authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election in which the FIS had taken a commanding lead.
